Archdocs lets a document owner gate changes through review and lets collaborators propose specific
1. **Doc-level review** - request review from named reviewers, who approve or request changes with a
comment. The document carries an aggregate review status.
2. **Element-level suggestions** - a collaborator proposes specific canvas edits as a delta; the owner
accepts or rejects them per element. (See the Suggestions section below.)
Anyone with the `review:request` permission (editors, admins, and owners) can request a review on a
document. Pick one or more reviewers from your organization's members; you cannot add yourself. Each
reviewer is notified in-app and by email.
A named reviewer with the `review:decide` permission opens the document and either **approves** or
**requests changes**, optionally leaving a comment. Only a named reviewer of that request can decide;
anyone else is refused even if they hold the permission. The requester is notified in-app and by
A review request has one of four statuses:
- **open** - the request is active and not every reviewer has approved.
- **changes_requested** - at least one reviewer requested changes.
The derived status follows a simple rule:
- If any reviewer requested changes, the status is **changes_requested** (this wins over approvals).
- Otherwise, if there is at least one reviewer and every reviewer approved, the status is
`cancelled` is a terminal state set explicitly by the requester; it is not derived from reviewer
decisions. The document header and the dashboard cards show the current status as a badge.
- `review:request` - request a review or cancel one. Granted to editors, admins, and owners.
- `review:decide` - record an approve / request-changes decision. Granted to editors, admins, and
owners, but only for a request you are a named reviewer of.
- Each reviewer is emailed (and notified in-app) when a review is requested.
- The requester is emailed (and notified in-app) on each decision, including the reviewer's comment.
Review notifications always deliver in-app and by email; there is no separate per-user review
Suggestions let a collaborator propose specific canvas edits without changing the live document. The
owner reviews each proposal and accepts or rejects it, per element.
Anyone with `docs:read` on a document can open **Suggest mode** from the document toolbar. On entry,
archdocs snapshots the current scene as the base. While suggest mode is on, your edits stay local:
they are not broadcast to other editors and do not change the saved document. When you are done,
choose **Submit suggestion**. archdocs diffs the live scene against the base snapshot and stores the
result as a suggestion (added, updated, and deleted elements), then restores your canvas to the base.
The proposal is now pending the owner's review. If you made no changes, nothing is submitted.
The captured `baseVersion` is the document's version at the time you entered suggest mode.
A user with `docs:write` sees open suggestions for the document, each rendered as a per-element diff:
For each suggestion the owner can **Accept all**, **Reject**, or **Accept** individual elements. When
an element is accepted, archdocs applies it through the same realtime path as a normal peer edit: the
change is merged into the document and broadcast as `architectureDocElementsApplied`, so every open
editor reconciles it into the live scene immediately. Rejecting a suggestion changes nothing on the
canvas; it just marks the proposal resolved.
Suggestions use coarse, document-level staleness. A suggestion is computed against the document
version at capture time. If the document moves to a newer version before the suggestion is accepted
(for example, another edit landed), accepting it marks the suggestion **stale** instead of applying
it, rather than risk merging against a base that no longer matches. Fine-grained per-element rebasing
is out of scope; resubmit the suggestion against the current document.
- Anyone with `docs:read` may enter suggest mode and submit a suggestion.
- Applying (accept) or rejecting a suggestion requires `docs:write`.
Archdocs ships a deep, full-text search across your architecture knowledge base. The Cmd+K dialog
searches document content, object metadata, and comment threads at once and returns grouped, ranked
results with highlighted snippets and one-click deep links.
| Docs     | name, description, and extracted diagram text |
| Objects  | name, kind, and metadata field values         |
Diagram text is extracted from the Excalidraw canvas on every save: plain text elements, ERD entity
titles and column names, API endpoint methods and paths (REST and gRPC), and sequence diagram
participant labels, message labels, and notes. This means a search for an endpoint path or a column
name finds the document that draws it, not just documents whose title happens to match.
Search is powered by PostgreSQL full-text search. Each indexed record stores a `tsvector` built with
weighted terms: the title is weight A and the body is weight B, so an exact title match outranks a
body-only match. Queries are parsed with `websearch_to_tsquery`, ranked with `ts_rank`, and the
highlighted snippet you see comes from `ts_headline` (the `<mark>` spans become the yellow
highlight). Results are grouped by type (Docs, Objects, Comments) and ordered by rank within each
Search never leaks content you cannot already see. Every query is scoped to your active organization
and runs through the same visibility rules as the rest of the app:
- A document (and its comments) appears only if it is non-private, or you created it, or you are the
organization owner, or you hold the `org:manage` permission. This mirrors `visibleDocsFilter`.
- Objects are scoped to your organization membership.
Soft-deleted documents, objects, and comments are removed from the index, so deleted content never
A dedicated `SearchDocument` table holds the search index. It is maintained automatically:
- Creating or updating a doc, object, or comment re-indexes that record.
- Soft-deleting a doc, object, or comment removes it from the index.
Index maintenance is best-effort and isolated: if an index write fails it is logged and swallowed,
so it can never break a save. To (re)build the index for existing data, run the backfill:
PostgreSQL full-text search is the right default: zero extra infrastructure, transactional
consistency with your data, and good relevance for the corpus sizes Archdocs targets. When a
workspace outgrows it (very large corpora, typo tolerance, synonyms, sub-50ms latency at scale), the
search engine can be swapped without touching any feature code.
All search flows through a single seam, the `SearchIndexProvider` interface:
`PgSearchProvider` is the only implementation today. To move to Meilisearch or Typesense:

Implementation commit: `daea97d7300cf2314d559ea5c58afc2a6cef5745` (`feat(api): trial local semantic task context behind org flag`). A subsequent documentation commit records this report and measurement artifacts. Nothing was pushed or merged. No ArchDocs MCP tools were called. The existing untracked `apps/api/.env.eval` was left untouched.

The logical flag is `task-context-semantic`. There is no existing server-side PostHog flag evaluation helper in the API (`getFeatureFlag`/`isFeatureEnabled` search found none). This implementation therefore uses the explicitly permitted fallback, `SEMANTIC_CONTEXT_ORG_IDS`, a comma-separated organization UUID allowlist. Unset/empty means off for everybody. It neither introduces a PostHog request nor sends task/document text outside the API process.

`@huggingface/transformers` is pinned to **3.8.1**. The model is `sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2`, revision **1110a243fdf4706b3f48f1d95db1a4f5529b4d41**, using the revision's unquantized `onnx/model.onnx`. No quantized variant is enabled. Tokenization explicitly truncates at sentence-transformers' 256-token limit; attention-mask mean pooling and L2 normalization follow inference. Explicit tokenization is necessary because the v3 feature-extraction pipeline ignores a call-level `max_length` option.

`semantic:model` fetches the six pinned files and checks their sizes and SHA256 digests against `scripts/semantic-model-manifest.json`. Docker runs this command during image build. Files reside under `apps/api/models/<revision>/`, separate from `dist` so `nest build` cannot erase them. Runtime sets `allowRemoteModels=false`, `local_files_only=true`, disables filesystem/browser caches, and points the model host at `127.0.0.1:1`. These switches follow [Transformers.js local-model configuration](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers.js/custom_usage). The Node CPU backend uses one intra-op and one inter-op thread.

The Docker base changes from Alpine to Debian bookworm slim because the native ONNX CPU binding requires glibc. Existing workspace package copies remain in place. `.dockerignore` excludes developer model caches, environment files, and node_modules; the image obtains its own checked model assets.

`SearchVector.vector` is **bytea**, containing 384 big-endian Float32 values: **1,536 vector bytes per block**, independent of host byte order. This avoids pgvector and Prisma's substantial real-array decoding cost. The initial real[] prototype measured approximately 0.6 seconds for full context on 5,000 blocks; switching to binary vectors materially reduced that cost. The schema also stores the requested entity/block/model/hash/heading fields, block prose, source generation, and an FK to SearchDocument. A database constraint checks dimension and byte length. The migration is ordered after the repository's existing supporting-document migrations.

Indexing reuses `passage.ts`'s exported block splitter. It removes the four-field design-doc metadata header, splits the journal per `Work Log entry N:` before splitting blocks, and embeds `title. heading: block`. Supporting-document prose is read without its optional title/kind metadata, retaining description and content; knowledge statements remain prose. A SHA256 of the complete embedding input lets unchanged blocks reuse vectors, even when their block indices move. Consequently a title/heading change also invalidates the embedding.

SearchIndexerService schedules eligible entities only for enabled organizations. HTTP work starts after response `finish`/`close`; non-HTTP indexing schedules a later event-loop turn. One background worker processes a coalescing queue capped at 1,000 entities, yielding between blocks. Queue overflow and failures are logged without rejecting document writes. Final replacement deletes and recreates an entity's rows in one transaction. Parent/source locks and a source recheck reject stale workers. FK cascades and domain deletion/archive/retirement/suppression triggers remove derived vectors, including a deleted design doc's supporting-document and knowledge-item vectors.

Retrieval reads at most the organization's most recent **20,000 current blocks**, with a one-row overflow probe and a cap warning. It obtains candidate visibility through **the existing `DeepSearchService.searchAll` and PgSearchProvider path**. An internal candidate-ID option replaces the lexical match predicate; the same organization, live entity/parent, private draft, location, archived, retired, and suppressed filters still run. Lexical snippet generation is skipped for this internal visibility check. Knowledge-item label filtering also remains in searchAll. Only IDs returned by that viewer-scoped path are scored or admitted to fusion. Hidden candidates never enter returned groups or their counts. The private-candidate unit and integration tests exercise this boundary.

The task is embedded once per semantic retrieval. Normalized dot products select each visible entity's best block, then entity ranks are fused with the existing deduplicated lexical hits using RRF `1/(60 + rank)`. Ties keep lexical insertion order. Existing grouping, authority ordering, scope rules, paging, and the API contract remain unchanged. Semantic-only discoveries receive `matched by meaning` and their best block passage, using the existing heading/cropping rules and 400-character cap. Model/retrieval failures fall back to lexical results.

With the flag off there are no semantic database/model calls. A unit test compares complete responses and Prisma/search call arguments with the original path. A separate executable comparison checks the ordinary provider SQL and bound parameters against the branch base: **byte-for-byte identical in all three tested modes** (default, task options, and status filter).
